title: CRLR/127/2018 of Indrash Gopal Kohli Vs Dr. Anita Gupta Alias Anita Kohli AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Revision No. 84 of 2018
Dr. Anita Gupta @ Anita Kohli & another ... Revisionists
Vs
State of Uttarakhand&another ... Respondents
With
Criminal Revision No. 127 of 2018
Indrash Gopal Kohli ... Revisionists
Vs
Dr. Anita Gupta @ Anita Kohli & another ... Respondents
Mr. Prabhakar Joshi, learned counsel for the revisionists.
Mr. Partiroop Pandey, learned A.G.A. for the State of Uttarakhand.
Mr. Parikshit Saini, learned counsel for the respondent/husband.
Hon'ble Manoj K. Tiwari, J.
Both the Criminal Revisions are directed against the
order dated 15.02.2018 passed by Family Court, Rishikesh,
Dehradun in Misc. Case No. 106 of 2014, under Section 125
Cr.P.C., therefore, both are being heard and decided together.
2. Criminal Revision No. 84 of 2018 has been filed by
Dr. Anita Gupta (wife) for enhancement of the amount granted
for maintaining her and her minor son. Criminal Revision No.
127 of 2018 has been filed by husband (Dr. Indrash Gopal
Kohli), who has challenged the order granting amount of `
4,000/- per month as maintenance to his wife and ` 3,000/-
per month for education of his minor son.
3. Factum of marriage is not disputed between the
parties and it is admitted to both that they got married as per
Hindu Rites on 25.05.2009 at Rishikesh (Dehradun). It is also
not disputed that one son was born out of this wedlock,
namely, Master Tihan Kohli on 07.03.2010. Since differences
arose between the parties soon after marriage, therefore a
divorce suit was filed by the husband being Original Suit No.
59 of 2010, which was ultimately dismissed by learned
Additional Judge, Family Court, Rishikesh.
4. In the year 2014, Dr. Anita Gupta filed an
application under Section 125 Cr.P.C. as wife of Mr. Indrash

2
Gopal Kohli and also as natural guardian of her minor son,
who is dependent upon her. In the application, she alleged that
soon after marriage, she was subjected to mental and physical
cruelty by her husband and in-laws and she was driven out of
her matrimonial home within three weeks of giving birth to
Master Tihan Kohli, although, she was facing number of health
complications at the relevant point of time. She further alleged
that she filed written statement in the divorce suit filed by her
husband and the suit was dismissed as withdrawn, then the
husband took her to her matrimonial home for some time and
thereafter again in March, 2013 she was driven out of her
matrimonial home and she is thereafter living with her parents
at Yamunanagar (Haryana). She stated in her application that
she is not having any source of income, as she is unable to
practice as Ayurvedic Doctor in Haryana, as she surrendered
her registration in State of Haryana for seeking registration in
State of Uttarakhand, where her application for registration is
still pending. She further stated that Mr. Indrash Gopal Kohli
is the only son of Dr. Chaman Lal Kohli, who is a rich man and
owns a factory besides Kohli Hospital and various other
business/ properties in Rishikesh. In the application, it was
further stated that her husband is managing the
factory/hospital and other business undertakings of his family
and is earning lakhs of rupees each month, therefore he is a
man of sufficient means. The wife claimed `30,000/- as
maintenance for herself and `30,000/- for
maintenance/education of her minor son.
5. The husband in his objection stated that his parents
gave love and affection to Dr. Anita Gupta after marriage and
permitted her to manage and look after the hospital as its
owner, but she started behaving as if the hospital is her
personal property and she also insisted that the hospital be

3
transferred in her name. In the objection, he further stated that
Dr. Anita Gupta is not a good lady and she was interested in
grabbing his family property. Regarding his income, he stated
that he is a part time employee in a school and he is also
serving as a part time Office Assistant in a firm and he is
earning `13,000/- per month as salary, while his wife is a
qualified doctor and she is serving in a Nursing Home and is
also engaged in private practice and thus is earning handsome
amount each month.
6. Learned Additional Judge, Family Court partly
allowed the application filed under Section 125 Cr.P.C. vide
order dated 15.02.2018 and directed the husband to pay
`4,000/- per month as maintenance to the wife and `3,000/-
per month to the minor son. This order has been challenged by
the husband as well as the wife in these revisions.
7. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused
the record.
8. The provision incorporated in Section 125 Cr.P.C. is
a benevolent one to protect the estranged wife from vagrancy,
so that she may not become victim of the society. The husband
is legally bound to maintain his wife, subject to fulfilling the
conditions mentioned in the provision that despite having
sufficient income, he has neglected to maintain his wife. The
first and foremost condition of invoking the provision is the
refusal/ neglect on the part of the husband to maintain his
wife. Learned court below has recorded a finding that the
husband has neglected to maintain his wife. No attempt was
made on behalf of the husband to dislodge said finding.
9. Learned Family Court assessed the income of Mr.
Indrash Kumar Kohli solely on the basis of income tax return
and the other documentary evidences brought on record by his

4
wife was completely ignored. It is unbelievable that the only
son of Dr. Chaman Lal Kohli, who owns a big hospital,
medicine factory and various other business/properties in
Rishikesh, would be forced to serve as part time employee in a
school or also a firm for making both ends meet, moreso when
it is nobody's case that Dr. Chaman Lal Kohli's relations with
his son are strained.
10. In today's time, tax avoidance and tax evasion is the
norm. The income tax returns of a person do not always reflect
his correct income, especially when the assessee is self
employed person. Reference may be made to a Division Bench
decision of Delhi High Court rendered in the case of Anupam
Gupta v. Sumeet Gupta in CM (M) 1718 of 2004, wherein the
High Court has held as under:-
"27. As held by the Supreme Court of India in the
case of Jasbir Kaur (Smt.) (supra), Courts have also
recognized the fact that spouses in the proceedings for
maintenance do not truthfully disclose their true
income and therefore some guess work on the part of
the Court is permissible. Further the Supreme Court
has also observed that "considering the diverse
claims made by the parties one inflating the income
and the other suppressing an element of conjecture
and guess work does enter for arriving at the income
of the husband. It cannot be done by any
mathematical precision".
28. It has been held in the case of Neelam Malhotra v.
Rajinder Malhotra and Ors. reported at AIR 1994
Delhi 234 that the income from family business may
be taken into account while deciding an application
for interim maintenance. Relevant portion reads as
under:
"However, the controversial issue is whether the
moveable and Immovable assets belonging to
the other defendants could also be taken into
consideration for determining the earning
capacity and social status of the husband
particularly when it is alleged that all the assets
acquired by the defendants, including defendant

5
NO.I, are out of the joint family business being
run under the name and style of M/s-Laxmi
Traders. It is urged by Ms. Geeta Mittal, learned
counsel for the plaintiff that coupled with the
fact that defendant No. 1 is admittedly having a
joint kitchen with other members of the family,
the statement of his account in the books of
account of the said firm leaves little room for
doubt that the business of the said concern is
being carried on by the brother of defendant No.
I for the benefit of the entire family, including
defendant No. I and, Therefore, the income of the
said firm should be taken into account not only
to determine the social status of defendant No.1
but also for fixing the quantum of interim
maintenance".
11. After considering the entire material on record,
learned Family Court, Rishikesh has recorded a finding that
Mr. Indrash Gopal Kohli has neglected to maintain his wife and
minor son, as he has not given any financial support to them.
The said finding has not been challenged by the husband and
the only submission made on his behalf is that the wife herself
is earning handsome amount, therefore, she is not entitled to
any maintenance. Learned Family Court has further recorded
a finding that wife is not practicing anywhere, therefore, she
does not have any source of income.
12. However, for ascertaining financial status of the
husband, learned Family Court relied solely upon his income
tax return for the year 2015-16. The documentary evidence
available on record, including the certificate of importer-exporter (Paper No. 45Ka/2), issued by Ministry of Commerce,
Government of India, was not considered at all. Perusal of
Paper No. 45ka/2 indicates that Mr. Indrash Gopal Kohli
(husband) is the manufacturer of Ayurvedic Herbal Medicines
and Food Supplements under the name of Aarogya Herbal
Remedies. Paper No. 45ka/10 and 45ka/11 indicates that
Aarogya Herbal Remedies, had exported Ayurvedic Nutritional

6
Food Supplements worth 10430 US$ and 10500 US$ to a firm
in Bucharest Romania. Thus, Family Court erred in relying
solely upon the income tax return of the husband in which he
has shown income of `1,68,000/- as salary from Aarogya
Herbal Remedies and income of `1,45,716/- from other
sources. Learned Family Court ought to have considered the
documentary evidence filed by the wife for assessing the
financial status of the husband.
13. Dr. Anita Gupta in her cross-examination had
categorically stated that her husband is running several
business including a Medicine Factory, Physiotherapy
Institute, Hospital and he has rental income also from
properties. She had further stated that her husband is not an
employee in Aarogya Herbal Remedies, but it belongs to his
father. This aspect appears to have been overlooked by
learned Family Court.
14. Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bhuwan
Mohan Singh Vs Meena & others reported in 2015 (6) SCC
353 held in para 2, as under:-
"Be it ingeminated that Section 125 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure (for short "the Code") was conceived to
ameliorate the agony, anguish, financial suffering of a
woman who left her matrimonial home for the reasons
provided in the provision so that some suitable
arrangements can be made by the court and she can
sustain herself and also her children if they are with her.
The concept of sustenance does not necessarily mean to
lead the life of an animal, feel like an unperson to be
thrown away from grace and roam for her basic
maintenance somewhere else. She is entitled in law to lead
a life in the similar manner as she would have lived in the
house of her husband. That is where the status and strata
come into play, and that is where the obligations of the
husband, in case of a wife, become a prominent one. In a
proceeding of this nature, the husband cannot take
subterfuges to deprive her of the benefit of living with
dignity. Regard being had to the solemn pledge at the time
of marriage and also in consonance with the statutory law

7
that governs the field, it is the obligation of the husband to
see that the wife does not become a destitute, a beggar. A
situation is not to be maladroitly created whereunder she is
compelled to resign to her fate and think of life "dust unto
dust". It is totally impermissible. In fact, it is the sacrosanct
duty to render the financial support even if the husband is
required to earn money with physical labour, if he is able-bodied. There is no escape route unless there is an order
from the court that the wife is not entitled to get
maintenance from the husband on any legally permissible
grounds."
15. It is admitted that apart from Dr. Anita Gupta and
her son - Master Tihan Kohli, there is no other dependent
family member of Mr. Indrash Gopal Kohli. Learned counsel
for the husband submits that wife is not entitled to any
maintenance, as she is highly qualified and she can earn
handsome amount from medical practice. The said submission
is without any substance. Learned Family Court, after
considering the material on record has arrived at a conclusion
that wife is not working anywhere, therefore, she is unable to
maintain herself and her son. It is settled position in law that
capacity to earn and actually earning are two separate things.
The contention of the husband is that the wife is possessing
Bachelor of Ayurvedic Medicine & Surgery qualification and is
earning about `60,000/- per month from medical practice,
however, he has failed to show any material that the wife is
gainfully employed or earning.
16. Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Chaturbhuj
vs. Sita Bai reported in (2008) 2 SCC 316 has held that wife
can claim maintenance even when she is earning, but her
income is insufficient to maintain her. Para 8 of the said
judgment is extracted below:-
"8. In an illustrative case where the wife was
surviving by begging, it would not amount to her
ability to maintain herself. It can also be not said that
the wife has been capable of earning but she was not
making an effort to earn. Whether the deserted wife

8
was unable to maintain herself, has to be decided on
the basis of the material placed on record. Where the
personal income of the wife is insufficient she can
claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. The test
is whether the wife is in a position to maintain herself
in the way she was used to in the place of her
husband. In Bhagwan Dutt v. Kamla Devi3 it was
observed that the wife should be in a position to
maintain a standard of living which is neither
luxurious nor penurious but what is consistent with
status of a family. The expression "unable to maintain
herself" does not mean that the wife must be
absolutely destitute before she can apply for
maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C."
18. It is settled position in law that a wife is entitled to
live in a similar status, as was enjoyed by her in her
matrimonial home. It is the duty of the courts to ensure that it
should not be a case that one spouse lives in a life of comfort
and luxury, while the other spouse lives a life of deprivation
and poverty. In the case of Jasbir Kaur Sehgal (Smt.) v.
District Judge, Dehradun & others reported in (1997) 7
SCC 7, it has been held as under:-
"8. No set formula can be laid for fixing the amount of
maintenance. It has, in the very nature of things, to
depend on the facts and circumstance of each case.
Some scope for liverage can, however, be always
there. Court has to consider the status of the parties,
their respective needs, capacity of the husband to pay
having regard to his reasonable expenses for his own
maintenance and of those he is obliged under the law
and statutory but involuntary payments or
deductions. The amount of maintenance fixed for the
wife should be such as she can live in reasonable
comfort considering her status and the mode of life
she was used to when she lived with her husband
and also that she does not feel handicapped in the
prosecution of her case. At the same time, the
amount so fixed cannot be excessive or extortionate.
In the circumstances of the present case we fix
maintenance pendente lite at the rate of Rs. 5,000/-
per month payable by respondent-husband to the
appellant-wife."

9
19. Further it has been noticed by the courts that
tendency of the spouse in proceedings for maintenance to not
truthfully disclose their true income. Thus, in such cases some
guess work on the part of the court is permissible. In the
present case, learned Additional Judge, Family Court,
Rishikesh has considered only income tax return of the
husband, while deciding the application under Section 125
Cr.P.C. A single of Delhi High Court in the case of Bharat
Hegde v. Saroj Hegde reported in 140 (2007 DLT 16, has
culled out eleven factors, which can be taken into
consideration for deciding application under Section 24 of
Hindu Marriage Act. Relevant and operative portion of which,
reads as under:-
"8. Unfortunately, in India, parties do not truthfully
reveal their income. For self employed persons or
persons employed in the unorganized sector, truthful
income never surfaces. Tax avoidance is the norm.
Tax compliance is the exception in this country.
Therefore, in determining the interim maintenance,
there cannot be mathematical exactitude. The court
has to take a general view. From the various judicial
precedents, the under noted 11 factors can be culled
out, which are to be taken into consideration while
deciding an application under Section 24 of the Hindu
Marriage Act. The same are:-
(1) Status of the parties.
(2) Reasonable wants of the claimant.
(3) The independent income and property of the
claimant.
(4) The number of persons, the non applicant has to
maintain.
(5) The amount should aid the applicant to live in a
similar life style as he/she enjoyed in the
matrimonial home.
(6) Non-applicant's liabilities, if any.
(7) Provisions for food clothing, shelter, education,
medical attendance and treatment etc. of the
applicant.
(8) Payment capacity of the non-applicant.
(9) Some guess work is not ruled out while
estimating the income of the non-applicant when
all the sources or correct sources are not
disclosed.

10
(10) The non-applicant to defray the cost of litigation.
(11) The amount awarded under Section 125 Cr.P.C.
is adjustable against the amount awarded
under Section 24 of the Act."
20. In the case of Neelam Malhotra v. Rajinder
Malhotra & others reported in AIR 1994 Delhi 234, Delhi
High Court has held that the income from family business may
be taken into account, while deciding an application for interim
maintenance. Relevant portion of the same reads as under:-
"However, the controversial issue is whether the
moveable and immovable assets belonging to the
other defendants could also be taken into
consideration for determining the earning capacity
and social status of the husband particularly when it
is alleged that all the assets acquired by the
defendants, including defendant No. 1, are out of the
joint family business being run under the name and
style of M/s Laxmi Traders. It is urged by Ms. Geeta
Mittal, learned counsel for the plaintiff that coupled
with the fact that defendant No. 1 is admittedly
having a joint kitchen with other members of the
family, the statement of his account in the books of
account of the said firm leaves little room for doubt
that the business of the said concern is being carried
on by the brother of defendant No. 1 for the benefit of
the entire family, including defendant No. 1 and
therefore, the income of the said firm should be taken
into account not only to determine the social status of
defendant No. 1 but also for fixing the quantum of
interim maintenance."
21. In the case of Shamima Farooqui V. Shahid Khan
reported in 2015(2) RCR (Criminal) 526 it has been held that
plea of husband that he is not doing job and has no means to
pay, cannot be accepted to deny the maintenance, these are
only bald excuses. In case, the husband is healthy, able bodied
and is in a position to support himself, he is under legal
obligation to support his wife as well. Hon'ble Supreme Court
has gone to the extent in saying that it is the obligation of the
husband to maintain his wife and he cannot be permitted to

11
plead that he is unable to maintain the wife due to financial
constraints as long as he is capable of earning.
22. Mr. Parikshit Saini, learned counsel for the husband
submits that learned Family Court has erred in awarding
maintenance from the date of application in the absence of any
reason for the same. This submission made by learned
counsel for the husband is bereft of any merit. Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of Shail Kumari Devi v. Krishan
Bhagwan Pathak reported in (2008) 9 SCC 632 has held, as
under:-
"42. Again, maintenance is a right which accrues to a
wife against her husband the minute the former gets
married to the latter. It is not only a moral obligation
but is also a legal duty cast upon the husband to
maintain his wife. Hence, whenever a wife does not
stay with her husband and claims maintenance, the
only question which the court is called upon to
consider is whether she was justified to live
separately from her husband and still claim
maintenance from him? If the reply is in the
affirmative, she is entitled to claim maintenance. It is,
therefore, open to the Magistrate to award
maintenance from the date of application and there is
nothing which requires recording of "special reasons"
though he must record reasons as envisaged by sub-section (6) of Section 354 of the Code in support of the
order passed by him.
43. We, therefore, hold that while deciding an
application under Section 125 of the Code, a
Magistrate is required to record reasons for granting
or refusing to grant maintenance to wives, children or
parents. Such maintenance can be awarded from the
date of the order, or, if so ordered, from the date of the
application for maintenance, as the case may be. For
awarding maintenance from the date of the
application, express order is necessary. No special
reasons, however, are required to be recorded by the
court. In our judgment, no such requirement can be
read in sub-section (1) of Section 125 of the Code in
absence of express provision to that effect."

12
23. In view of the aforesaid discussion, it is apparent
that reliance placed by Family Court on income tax return
alone for ascertaining the income of the husband is not proper.
Since there is tendency amongst individual to disclose less
income in order to avoid income tax liability and also with a
view to avoid liability to pay maintenance, therefore, income
tax return cannot be the sole basis for ascertaining the paying
capacity of the husband, as held by learned Single Judge of
Delhi High Court in the case of Bharat Hegde v. Saroj Hegde
(supra).
24. Since learned Family Court has not considered the
entire evidence available on record, regarding income of the
husband from various sources, therefore, the impugned order
is liable to be set aside.
25. Accordingly, impugned order dated 15.02.2018 is
set aside. The matter is remitted back to learned Family
Court, Rishikesh, District Dehradun to decide the application
under Section 125 Cr.P.C. afresh, after considering the entire
evidence available on record, within four months from the date
of production of certified copy of this judgment.
26. With the aforesaid direction, criminal revisions
stand disposed of.
(Manoj K. Tiwari, J.)
21.08.2019
Aswal
